solution:
For a concave mirror \(f = R/2 = -36/2 = -18\,\text{cm}\), and the object is at \(u = -27\,\text{cm}\).

Mirror equation \(\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\):

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{-18} - \dfrac{1}{-27} = \dfrac{-3 + 2}{54} = -\dfrac{1}{54}\)

so \(v = -54\,\text{cm}\). The negative sign puts the image on the same side as the object, so it is REAL and the screen must be placed there.

Magnification \(m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{(-54)}{(-27)} = -2\)

The negative \(m\) means the image is inverted, and \(|m| = 2\) means it is magnified. Size of image \(= 2 \times 2.5 = 5.0\,\text{cm}\).

If the candle is moved closer to the mirror, \(|u|\) decreases towards \(|f| = 18\,\text{cm}\); then \(|v|\) grows without limit, so the screen must be moved FARTHER from the mirror. Once the candle is nearer than \(18\,\text{cm}\) the image becomes virtual and cannot be collected on a screen at all.

Screen at \(54\,\text{cm}\) from the mirror, on the same side as the candle; the image is real, inverted and magnified, of size \(5.0\,\text{cm}\). Moving the candle closer moves the screen farther away.

For a convex mirror \(f = +15\,\text{cm}\), and \(u = -12\,\text{cm}\).

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{15} + \dfrac{1}{12} = \dfrac{4 + 5}{60} = \dfrac{3}{20}\)

so \(v = +6.67\,\text{cm}\). The positive sign puts the image BEHIND the mirror, so it is virtual and erect.

\(m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{6.67}{-12} = +0.556 = \dfrac{5}{9}\)

Size of image \(= \dfrac{5}{9} \times 4.5 = 2.5\,\text{cm}\).

As the needle is moved farther away, \(u \to -\infty\) and \(\dfrac{1}{v} \to \dfrac{1}{f}\), so the image moves towards the focus (\(v \to 15\,\text{cm}\)) but never beyond it, while \(m \to 0\) — the image steadily shrinks.

Image \(6.7\,\text{cm}\) behind the mirror, virtual and erect; \(m = 5/9\), size \(2.5\,\text{cm}\).

For near-normal viewing, refractive index \(= \dfrac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}}\).

\(n_w = \dfrac{12.5}{9.4} = 1.33\)

With the liquid of \(n = 1.63\) filled to the same real depth \(12.5\,\text{cm}\), the new apparent depth is

\(\dfrac{12.5}{1.63} = 7.67\,\text{cm}\)

The needle now appears \(9.4 - 7.67 = 1.73\,\text{cm}\) higher than before, so the microscope must be moved UP (towards the liquid surface) by that much to refocus.

Refractive index of water \(= 1.33\); the microscope must be raised by about \(1.7\,\text{cm}\).

Snell's law gives the refractive index of the denser medium with respect to air as \(n = \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}\).

From Fig. 9.27(a), light goes air \(\to\) glass with \(i = 60^\circ\), \(r = 35^\circ\):

\(n_{ga} = \dfrac{\sin 60^\circ}{\sin 35^\circ} = \dfrac{0.8660}{0.5736} = 1.51\)

From Fig. 9.27(b), light goes air \(\to\) water with \(i = 60^\circ\). Taking the refraction angle to be \(41^\circ\),

\(n_{wa} = \dfrac{\sin 60^\circ}{\sin 41^\circ} = \dfrac{0.8660}{0.6561} = 1.32\)

(The angle printed in Fig. 9.27(b) is \(47^\circ\), which would give \(n_{wa} = 1.18\) — not the refractive index of water. This same exercise set states water's refractive index as \(1.33\) three separate times: it is the answer to Ex 9.3 and it is given outright in Ex 9.5 and Ex 9.6. The printed \(47^\circ\) is therefore a misprint for \(41^\circ\), which is exactly the angle Snell's law gives for \(60^\circ\) incidence into water.)

For the water-glass interface, the relative refractive index is

\(n_{gw} = \dfrac{n_{ga}}{n_{wa}} = \dfrac{1.51}{1.32} = 1.14\)

Now apply Snell's law at the water-glass interface of Fig. 9.27(c) with \(i = 45^\circ\) in water:

\(\sin r = \dfrac{\sin 45^\circ}{n_{gw}} = \dfrac{0.7071}{1.144} = 0.618\)

\(r = \sin^{-1}(0.618) = 38.2^\circ\)

The angle of refraction in the glass is about \(38^\circ\).
_note: BOOK DEFECT (figure, not stem). Fig. 9.27(b) prints 47 deg for the refraction of a 60 deg ray entering water. That yields n_wa = sin60/sin47 = 1.184, which is not water. 41 deg yields 1.3200. The chapter's own exercises state n_water = 1.33 three times (Ex 9.3's answer; given in Ex 9.5 and Ex 9.6), so the inconsistency is demonstrable WITHOUT the answer key. Solved for the sensible intended form (41 deg) per the brief; as printed (47 deg) the chain gives n_gw = 1.275 and r = 33.7 deg.

solution:
Light can escape the water surface only where it strikes at less than the critical angle; beyond that it is totally internally reflected. The escaping light therefore emerges through a circle centred vertically above the bulb.

Critical angle: \(\sin i_c = \dfrac{1}{n} = \dfrac{1}{1.33} = 0.752\), so \(i_c = 48.8^\circ\).

A ray leaving the bulb at \(i_c\) meets the surface at a horizontal distance \(r\) from the axis, where the depth \(h = 80\,\text{cm}\) gives

\(r = h \tan i_c = 80 \times \tan 48.8^\circ = 80 \times 1.140 = 91.2\,\text{cm} = 0.912\,\text{m}\)

Area of the circle:

\(A = \pi r^{2} = \pi (0.912)^{2} = 2.61\,\text{m}^{2}\)

The light emerges through a circular patch of area about \(2.6\,\text{m}^{2}\).

At minimum deviation the prism formula is

\(n = \dfrac{\sin\left(\dfrac{A + D_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)}\)

With \(A = 60^\circ\) and \(D_m = 40^\circ\):

\(n = \dfrac{\sin 50^\circ}{\sin 30^\circ} = \dfrac{0.766}{0.5} = 1.53\)

When the prism is immersed in water the RELATIVE refractive index of glass with respect to water is what enters the formula:

\(n_{gw} = \dfrac{1.53}{1.33} = 1.152\)

\(\sin\left(\dfrac{60^\circ + D_m'}{2}\right) = n_{gw}\sin 30^\circ = 1.152 \times 0.5 = 0.576\)

\(\dfrac{60^\circ + D_m'}{2} = \sin^{-1}(0.576) = 35.2^\circ\)

\(D_m' = 70.4^\circ - 60^\circ = 10.4^\circ\)

Refractive index of the prism \(= 1.53\); the new angle of minimum deviation in water is about \(10^\circ\).

For a double-convex lens with both faces of the same radius \(R\), the Cartesian sign convention gives \(R_1 = +R\) and \(R_2 = -R\).

Lens maker's formula:

\(\dfrac{1}{f} = (n - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right) = (n - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R} + \dfrac{1}{R}\right) = \dfrac{2(n - 1)}{R}\)

So \(R = 2(n-1)f\).

With \(n = 1.55\) and \(f = 20\,\text{cm}\):

\(R = 2(0.55)(20) = 22\,\text{cm}\)

The required radius of curvature is \(22\,\text{cm}\).

The beam is already converging towards P when the lens intercepts it, so P acts as a VIRTUAL OBJECT: it lies on the outgoing side of the lens and \(u = +12\,\text{cm}\).

Lens equation \(\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\).

(a) Convex lens, \(f = +20\,\text{cm}\):

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{20} + \dfrac{1}{12} = \dfrac{3 + 5}{60} = \dfrac{2}{15}\)

\(v = 7.5\,\text{cm}\)

The converging lens bends the beam more, so it meets the axis sooner.

(b) Concave lens, \(f = -16\,\text{cm}\):

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{16} + \dfrac{1}{12} = \dfrac{-3 + 4}{48} = \dfrac{1}{48}\)

\(v = 48\,\text{cm}\)

The diverging lens delays the convergence.

(a) The beam converges \(7.5\,\text{cm}\) from the lens, on its far side (a real image).
(b) The beam converges \(48\,\text{cm}\) from the lens, on its far side (a real image).

Concave lens: \(f = -21\,\text{cm}\); object at \(u = -14\,\text{cm}\), size \(3.0\,\text{cm}\).

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{21} - \dfrac{1}{14} = -\dfrac{2 + 3}{42} = -\dfrac{5}{42}\)

\(v = -8.4\,\text{cm}\)

The negative \(v\) puts the image on the SAME side as the object, so it is virtual and erect.

\(m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{-8.4}{-14} = +0.6\)

Size of image \(= 0.6 \times 3.0 = 1.8\,\text{cm}\) — diminished.

As the object is moved further away, \(u \to -\infty\) and \(\dfrac{1}{v} \to \dfrac{1}{f}\): the image creeps towards the focus (\(|v| \to 21\,\text{cm}\)) but never beyond it, while \(m \to 0\) so the image keeps shrinking.

The image is virtual, erect and diminished, \(8.4\,\text{cm}\) from the lens on the object's side, of size \(1.8\,\text{cm}\).

For thin lenses in contact the powers add, i.e. \(\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{f_1} + \dfrac{1}{f_2}\).

Here \(f_1 = +30\,\text{cm}\) (convex) and \(f_2 = -20\,\text{cm}\) (concave):

\(\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{30} - \dfrac{1}{20} = \dfrac{2 - 3}{60} = -\dfrac{1}{60}\)

\(f = -60\,\text{cm}\)

A negative focal length means the combination diverges light.

The combination has focal length \(60\,\text{cm}\) and is a DIVERGING lens (\(f = -60\,\text{cm}\), power \(-1.67\,\text{D}\)).

\(f_o = 2.0\,\text{cm}\), \(f_e = 6.25\,\text{cm}\), separation \(L = 15\,\text{cm}\). Work backwards from the eyepiece.

(a) Final image at the near point, \(v_e = -25\,\text{cm}\):

\(\dfrac{1}{u_e} = \dfrac{1}{v_e} - \dfrac{1}{f_e} = -\dfrac{1}{25} - \dfrac{1}{6.25} = -0.04 - 0.16 = -0.20\)

\(u_e = -5\,\text{cm}\), so the objective's image lies \(5\,\text{cm}\) before the eyepiece, i.e. \(v_o = 15 - 5 = 10\,\text{cm}\).

\(\dfrac{1}{u_o} = \dfrac{1}{v_o} - \dfrac{1}{f_o} = \dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{2} = -0.40\), so \(u_o = -2.5\,\text{cm}\).

Magnifying power \(= \left|\dfrac{v_o}{u_o}\right|\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}\right) = \dfrac{10}{2.5}\left(1 + \dfrac{25}{6.25}\right) = 4 \times 5 = 20\)

(b) Final image at infinity: the objective's image must sit at the eyepiece's focus, so \(u_e = -6.25\,\text{cm}\) and \(v_o = 15 - 6.25 = 8.75\,\text{cm}\).

\(\dfrac{1}{u_o} = \dfrac{1}{8.75} - \dfrac{1}{2} = -0.3857\), so \(u_o = -2.59\,\text{cm}\).

Magnifying power \(= \left|\dfrac{v_o}{u_o}\right| \times \dfrac{D}{f_e} = \dfrac{8.75}{2.59} \times 4 = 13.5\)

(a) Object \(2.5\,\text{cm}\) from the objective; magnifying power \(20\).
(b) Object \(2.59\,\text{cm}\) from the objective; magnifying power \(13.5\).

Convert to centimetres: \(f_o = 8.0\,\text{mm} = 0.8\,\text{cm}\), \(u_o = -9.0\,\text{mm} = -0.9\,\text{cm}\), \(f_e = 2.5\,\text{cm}\), \(D = 25\,\text{cm}\).

Objective:

\(\dfrac{1}{v_o} = \dfrac{1}{f_o} + \dfrac{1}{u_o} = \dfrac{1}{0.8} - \dfrac{1}{0.9} = 1.25 - 1.111 = 0.1389\)

\(v_o = 7.2\,\text{cm}\)

Eyepiece, with the final image at the near point (\(v_e = -25\,\text{cm}\)):

\(\dfrac{1}{u_e} = \dfrac{1}{v_e} - \dfrac{1}{f_e} = -\dfrac{1}{25} - \dfrac{1}{2.5} = -0.44\)

\(u_e = -2.27\,\text{cm}\)

The objective's image must fall \(2.27\,\text{cm}\) before the eyepiece, so the lens separation is

\(v_o + |u_e| = 7.2 + 2.27 = 9.47\,\text{cm}\)

Magnifying power:

\(m = \left|\dfrac{v_o}{u_o}\right|\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}\right) = \dfrac{7.2}{0.9}\left(1 + \dfrac{25}{2.5}\right) = 8 \times 11 = 88\)

Separation between the lenses \(= 9.47\,\text{cm}\); magnifying power \(= 88\).

For a telescope in normal adjustment (final image at infinity) the magnifying power is

\(m = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e} = \dfrac{144}{6.0} = 24\)

In normal adjustment the objective's focus coincides with the eyepiece's focus, so the tube length is

\(L = f_o + f_e = 144 + 6.0 = 150\,\text{cm}\)

Magnifying power \(= 24\); separation between objective and eyepiece \(= 150\,\text{cm}\).

(a) \(f_o = 15\,\text{m} = 1500\,\text{cm}\) and \(f_e = 1.0\,\text{cm}\).

\(m = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e} = \dfrac{1500}{1.0} = 1500\)

(b) The moon subtends, at the objective, the angle

\(\theta = \dfrac{\text{diameter of moon}}{\text{radius of lunar orbit}} = \dfrac{3.48 \times 10^{6}}{3.8 \times 10^{8}} = 9.16 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{rad}\)

The objective forms the image in its focal plane, so the image subtends the same angle at the objective and has diameter

\(d = f_o\,\theta = 15 \times 9.16 \times 10^{-3} = 0.137\,\text{m} = 13.7\,\text{cm}\)

(a) Angular magnification \(= 1500\).
(b) Diameter of the moon's image formed by the objective \(= 13.7\,\text{cm}\).

Concave mirror, so \(f < 0\); the object is in front, so \(u < 0\). "Between \(f\) and \(2f\)" means \(2f < u < f\).

From \(\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\),

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{u - f}{uf}\)

Since \(u < f < 0\), the numerator \(u - f < 0\); and \(uf > 0\) because both are negative. Hence \(\dfrac{1}{v} < 0\), so \(v < 0\): the image is on the same side as the object, i.e. REAL.

For its position, invert:

\(v = \dfrac{uf}{u - f}\)

Write \(u = af\) with \(1 < a < 2\) (this is exactly the condition \(2f < u < f\)). Then

\(v = \dfrac{af \cdot f}{af - f} = \dfrac{af}{a - 1}\)

so \(|v| = \dfrac{a}{a-1}|f|\). For \(1 < a < 2\) the factor \(\dfrac{a}{a-1} > 2\) (it equals \(2\) at \(a = 2\) and increases without limit as \(a \to 1\)).

Therefore \(|v| > 2|f|\): the image lies beyond \(2f\).

Hence an object between \(f\) and \(2f\) of a concave mirror gives a real image beyond \(2f\).

Convex mirror, so \(f > 0\); a real object in front of it has \(u < 0\).

From the mirror equation,

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u}\)

Here \(\dfrac{1}{f} > 0\) because \(f > 0\), and \(-\dfrac{1}{u} > 0\) because \(u < 0\). A sum of two positive terms is positive, so

\(\dfrac{1}{v} > 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad v > 0\)

A positive \(v\) means the image lies BEHIND the mirror, where no light actually goes — it is virtual.

Nothing in this argument used the size of \(|u|\): it holds for every object position with \(u < 0\).

Hence a convex mirror always forms a virtual image, wherever the object is placed.

Convex mirror: \(f > 0\), object \(u < 0\). Write \(|u| = -u\).

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{1}{|u|}\)

POSITION. Because \(\dfrac{1}{|u|} > 0\),

\(\dfrac{1}{v} > \dfrac{1}{f} \quad\Rightarrow\quad 0 < v < f\)

so the image always lies between the pole and the focus, behind the mirror.

SIZE. Because \(\dfrac{1}{f} > 0\),

\(\dfrac{1}{v} > \dfrac{1}{|u|} \quad\Rightarrow\quad v < |u|\)

and the magnification is

\(|m| = \left|\dfrac{v}{u}\right| = \dfrac{v}{|u|} < 1\)

so the image is always smaller than the object.

Hence the virtual image in a convex mirror is always diminished and always lies between the focus and the pole.

Concave mirror: \(f < 0\). The object lies between the pole and the focus, so \(f < u < 0\), i.e. \(|u| < |f|\).

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{|f|} + \dfrac{1}{|u|} = \dfrac{|f| - |u|}{|f||u|}\)

Since \(|u| < |f|\) the numerator is positive, so \(\dfrac{1}{v} > 0\) and \(v > 0\): the image lies behind the mirror and is VIRTUAL.

Inverting,

\(v = \dfrac{|f||u|}{|f| - |u|}\)

and the magnification is

\(m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{v}{|u|} = \dfrac{|f|}{|f| - |u|}\)

The denominator \(|f| - |u|\) is positive and strictly less than \(|f|\), so \(m > 1\). Being positive, \(m\) also shows the image is erect.

Hence an object between the pole and the focus of a concave mirror gives a virtual, erect and enlarged image.

Looking almost normally through a parallel-sided slab of thickness \(t\) and refractive index \(n\), the object appears raised by the normal shift

\(\Delta = t\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{n}\right)\)

With \(t = 15\,\text{cm}\) and \(n = 1.5\):

\(\Delta = 15\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{1.5}\right) = 15\left(1 - 0.667\right) = 15 \times 0.333 = 5.0\,\text{cm}\)

The expression contains only \(t\) and \(n\) — the \(50\,\text{cm}\) viewing distance does not enter, and neither does how far the slab sits from the pin or from the eye. Physically, the slab displaces every paraxial ray sideways by the same amount wherever it is placed in the path, so the apparent shift is unchanged.

The pin appears raised by \(5.0\,\text{cm}\), and the answer does NOT depend on the location of the slab (for near-normal viewing).

Light entering the flat end face at angle \(i\) to the axis is refracted to angle \(r\) inside the fibre, and then strikes the cylindrical wall at angle \(i' = 90^\circ - r\) to the wall's normal. Total internal reflection at the wall needs \(i' > i_c'\), where \(i_c'\) is the critical angle for the core-cladding pair.

(a) Core \(n = 1.68\), cladding \(n = 1.44\):

\(\sin i_c' = \dfrac{1.44}{1.68} = 0.857 \quad\Rightarrow\quad i_c' = 59^\circ\)

So we need \(i' > 59^\circ\), i.e. \(r < 90^\circ - 59^\circ = 31^\circ\).

The largest entry angle is the one giving \(r_{max} = 31^\circ\):

\(\sin i_{max} = 1.68 \sin 31^\circ = 1.68 \times 0.515 = 0.865 \quad\Rightarrow\quad i_{max} = 60^\circ\)

All rays entering within \(0 < i < 60^\circ\) of the axis are totally reflected along the pipe.

(b) With no covering the cladding is air, \(n = 1\):

\(\sin i_c' = \dfrac{1}{1.68} = 0.595 \quad\Rightarrow\quad i_c' = 36.5^\circ\)

Now take the most extreme entry, grazing incidence \(i = 90^\circ\): \(\sin r = \dfrac{\sin 90^\circ}{1.68} = 0.595\), so \(r = 36.5^\circ\) and \(i' = 90^\circ - 36.5^\circ = 53.5^\circ\). Since even this smallest possible \(i'\) already exceeds \(i_c' = 36.5^\circ\), every other ray does too.

(a) Rays making any angle in the range \(0 < i < 60^\circ\) with the axis suffer total internal reflection.
(b) Without the covering, ALL rays entering the pipe (any \(i\) from \(0^\circ\) to \(90^\circ\)) suffer total internal reflection.
